clue.text: Allegorist blasted senator?

indicators.note: Something blasted has been blown apart, and the pieces never come down in the order they went up.

blocks.note: the ten letters of ALLEGORIST, laid out afresh

explanation.walkthrough: Two ten-letter words made of one set of letters, and the question mark is doing real work: it admits that only some lawmakers are senators.
explanation.definitionFit: senator? → LEGISLATOR: definition by example, since a senator is one member of a law-making chamber and MPs and congressmen qualify just as well.

clue.text: Tip one of 13, perhaps

blocks.note: a ship leaning over to one side does this verb — the tilt, not the topple
solve 13 down first: each of those documents is an itemised run of things

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman likes a cross-reference, and it always costs you a second clue: 13 down has to fall before the second half of this one means anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Tip → LIST, the lean of a ship rather than a hint; one of 13 → LIST by example, a spec sheet being one itemised run of entries.

clue.text: Disheartened, merchandise is Mars etc

indicators.note: A word that has lost heart has lost the letter at its very centre, not its courage.

blocks.note: merchandise is GOODS, and the middle letter of those five is taken out

explanation.walkthrough: Mars is a planet on the surface and a Roman deity underneath, and the little 'etc' is what makes the definition plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Mars etc → GODS: definition by example in the plural, Mars being the Roman god of war and 'etc' calling up Jupiter, Venus and the rest.

clue.text: Columbus grappling with eel that's very small

indicators.note: Two bodies locked together and thrashing about end up in a heap, which is what the letters beside this do.

blocks.note: the eleven letters of COLUMBUS and EEL, dealt out again

explanation.walkthrough: A long anagram is friendlier than it looks: count the fodder first, and eight letters plus three is exactly the eleven the grid is asking for.
explanation.definitionFit: that's very small → SUBMOLECULE: a part of a molecule, so the word names something below even molecular scale.

clue.text: Pardon? First couple of letters complete a crossword?

indicators.note: A couple is two, and the first two of anything are the pair at the very front of the sequence.

blocks.note: the letters meant are the alphabet's own, whose opening pair is A and B
to complete a crossword is to solve it

explanation.walkthrough: Two question marks and neither does the same job: the first is the surface saying 'what?', the second admits that solving is only one way to finish a grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Pardon → ABSOLVE: the formal sense of clearing someone of a charge, the priest's and the judge's word rather than the polite one.

clue.text: Trim hospital employee

blocks.note: the adjective: neat, everything in its place and nothing sticking out
the noun: the ward attendant who moves patients and equipment about

explanation.walkthrough: A three-word clue splits after the first word, which is the hardest split to see — 'trim' looks as though it belongs to the employee.
explanation.definitionFit: Trim → ORDERLY as an adjective meaning tidy; hospital employee → ORDERLY as a noun, the attendant who keeps a ward running.

clue.text: Give out prison sentence - in recess?

indicators.note: A recess is a space set back into a wall, so whatever sits in one has been pushed backwards.

blocks.note: a prison sentence is TIME — doing time — and set back it reads the other way round

explanation.walkthrough: TIME is the crossword's standard prison sentence, and a four-letter word that spells something else backwards will nearly always be asked to.
explanation.definitionFit: Give out → EMIT: the technical verb for sending something out from a source, what a lamp does with light or a chimney with smoke.

clue.text: Pieces of rock opera with ceremonies in which hero regularly crushed

indicators.note: This points back at everything just assembled, so the next letters drop inside it rather than line up after it.
Crush letters out of a word at fixed intervals and what stays standing is every other one.

blocks.note: New York's Metropolitan Opera is the Met
crush out the h and the r and hErO leaves its second and fourth letters
ceremonies are rites

explanation.walkthrough: The definition stops at 'rock', though the surface wants you to read 'rock opera' as one thing. MET for the Metropolitan is the abbreviation worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: Pieces of rock → METEORITES: the lumps of space debris that survive the fall to earth, so the plain phrase is literally what they are.

clue.text: Spooner's beloved sailing vessel? That was ages ago

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner traded the opening sounds of two words, so his name alone is the instruction to swap them.

blocks.note: a beloved is a dear, and Spooner hands its D over in exchange for a Y
a sailing vessel is a yacht, said 'yot', and it takes the D that dear gave up

explanation.walkthrough: The article comes free: nobody says 'year dot' without a 'the' in front of it, so the phrase arrives whole once the swap is made.
explanation.definitionFit: ages ago → THE YEAR DOT: the idiom names the earliest date anyone can imagine, and English uses it to mean as far back as memory goes.

clue.text: Yes, biddies sauntering two abreast

indicators.note: To saunter is to wander with no route in mind, and letters that wander do not come back in the order they set off in.

blocks.note: the ten letters of YES BIDDIES, dealt out again

explanation.walkthrough: 'Biddies' does all the misdirection: it summons a pair of gossiping old women strolling along, which is very nearly the picture the answer paints.
explanation.definitionFit: two abreast → SIDE BY SIDE: the marching phrase for a pair level with one another rather than one trailing behind.

clue.text: Source of irritation: pious type with Biblical term for you

blocks.note: a pious type is a saint, shortened to ST in front of a name
YE is how the King James Bible addresses you

explanation.walkthrough: ST for saint and YE for you are two of the crossword's steadiest abbreviations, and the colon is the only joint the clue needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Source of irritation → STYE: the swollen lump on an eyelid, named here by the discomfort it causes rather than by what it is.

clue.text: Arrested pacifist; one might say 'coo!'

blocks.note: to collar somebody is to arrest them, the policeman's verb
in politics the dove wants peace and the hawk wants war

explanation.walkthrough: Hawks and doves are the standing pair for warmongers and peacemakers, and the exclamation at the end is a bird's call rather than surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: one might say 'coo!' → COLLARED DOVE: the bird is defined by its voice, that soft repeated note being what everyone knows it for.

clue.text: Less enthused as date vomited all over the place

indicators.note: Something all over the place has no arrangement left, which is exactly what the letters beside it are asked to lose.

blocks.note: the eleven letters of DATE VOMITED, brought back in a new order

explanation.walkthrough: The setter splits a phrase you know: 'vomited all over the place' reads as one thing, yet only the last four words give the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Less enthused → DEMOTIVATED: the de- prefix strips drive away, so the keenness was there first and has since been taken off.

clue.text: Speech sets out iterated criteria

indicators.note: Out of true, out of shape, out of order: this little word carries the sense of an arrangement that no longer holds.

blocks.note: the ten letters of SPEECH SETS, re-dealt

explanation.walkthrough: Watch where the instruction sits: 'sets' belongs to the letters and only 'out' does the shuffling, which is why 'sets out' reads so innocently.
explanation.definitionFit: iterated criteria → SPEC SHEETS: a specification sheet runs through, point by point, every standard the product has to meet.

clue.text: Once again, making fun

blocks.note: RE- is the prefix English puts on anything done over
the making of a thing is its creation

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the hyphen you cannot see: built as re-creation it is making something over, read as one word it is what you do on a day off.
explanation.definitionFit: fun → RECREATION: the formal word for off-duty time, so 'fun' names the point of the activity rather than the activity itself.

clue.text: Herald in quiet decline

blocks.note: p is piano on a score, the musician's mark for quiet
to recede is to decline, as a tide or a hairline does

explanation.walkthrough: P for quiet comes from music, where piano means softly — one of the first abbreviations to bank, because it turns up most weeks.
explanation.definitionFit: Herald → PRECEDE: to herald a thing is to come before it and announce it, and the answer keeps the coming-before while dropping the announcing.

clue.text: After year, uncapped premium adjusted: more attractive

indicators.note: This says where to stand rather than what to do: everything else falls in behind, so the year goes first.
A cap sits on top of a thing, so a word uncapped has had the letter at its head taken off.
To adjust something is to shift its parts until they sit differently, and letters shifted like that come out in a new order.

blocks.note: y is the standard abbreviation for year
premium without its cap is REMIUM, and those six letters rearrange to UMMIER

explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncapped' beheads rather than shortens, and knowing which end of a word an instruction eats is half the work in clues like this.
explanation.definitionFit: more attractive → YUMMIER: the nursery word for delicious, stretched by adults to mean good-looking, with the comparative matching the -er.

clue.text: Blimey: point at end of game is rotten

indicators.note: The end of a thing is where it stops, so the piece sent there comes last and not first.

blocks.note: cor is the exclamation blimey stands in for
the game is rugby union, RU on any fixture list
pt is the everyday abbreviation for point

explanation.walkthrough: Three scraps of shorthand in a row — an exclamation, a sport and a measurement — while the surface pretends to be somebody watching a match.
explanation.definitionFit: rotten → CORRUPT: the moral sense of the word, a rotten official rather than rotten fruit, which is the decay the answer names.

clue.text: Primarily: tile; equally, small stone enhancing Roman art?

definitions.text: Primarily: tile; equally, small stone enhancing Roman art?

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so what is wanted from each word after it is the letter it starts with.

blocks.clueFragment: tile; equally, small stone enhancing Roman art
blocks.note: the opening letters of those seven words, taken in order

explanation.walkthrough: Seven words, seven initials — and the sentence supplying them is also a fair description of the thing, which is what lifts this above a plain acrostic.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a tessera is the little cube of a mosaic, a tile that is equally a stone, set into Roman floors.

clue.text: Busy month; egomaniac not seen throughout

indicators.note: If a thing cannot be seen all the way through, only a stretch of it shows — and a stretch is all you take.

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively, starting inside 'month' and finishing inside 'egomaniac'

explanation.walkthrough: A hidden word straddling a semicolon is beautifully disguised, because punctuation tells the eye to stop at the very place the answer carries on.
explanation.definitionFit: Busy → ON THE GO: the idiom for somebody moving from one task straight to the next, busy in the sense of never sitting down.

clue.text: A little alligator bit a lamprey that's going around

indicators.note: A little of something is a portion of it left as it stands, so one unbroken run of the letters that follow is what is being offered.

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively, spanning the tail of 'alligator', all of 'bit' and 'a', and the front of 'lamprey'

explanation.walkthrough: The eye reads whole words before it reads letters, and a word as long as 'alligator' can hide most of an answer in its own tail.
explanation.definitionFit: going around → ORBITAL: the adjective for anything that circles, whether a satellite's path or the motorway that rings a city.

clue.text: Gosh, cast earlier mentioned to include Poles

indicators.note: To include is to take a thing in, so the letters named next go inside what has already been built.

blocks.note: to cast something is to heave it
N and S are the two poles, north and south
what a document mentioned earlier is the above, as in the above-named

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here is theatrical: 'cast' is the verb to throw, and 'the above' is what legal and academic English calls whatever it said earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: Gosh → HEAVENS ABOVE: both are exclamations of surprise, the answer being the full pious version that 'gosh' politely trims down.

clue.text: Loudly trumpeted: that's indecent

indicators.note: Said out loud, so what matters is the noise a word makes and not the way it is spelt.

blocks.note: to trumpet a thing is to blow a horn about it, so trumpeted is BLEW — and that sound is written the other way here

explanation.walkthrough: A past tense is a favourite hiding place for a homophone: these two words are four letters apart on the page and identical in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: indecent → BLUE: the settled English sense of smut — a blue joke, a blue film — rather than the colour or the low mood.

clue.text: Maybe Murdoch is memoirist? Not entirely

indicators.note: Not entirely means you are not being handed the whole of it, so take only the part that is wanted.

blocks.note: the letters sit consecutively in the middle of 'memoirist'

explanation.walkthrough: Iris Murdoch wrote the novels, and 'maybe' is there because a bare surname could just as easily belong to Rupert.
explanation.definitionFit: Maybe Murdoch → IRIS: definition by example, one Murdoch among several, with 'maybe' the setter admitting that the surname alone does not pick her out.

clue.text: Everyman's beginning to get very off-colour, mostly wrong

indicators.note: A word's beginning is the single letter it starts with, and the setter has offered his own name to supply one.
Mostly is most but not all, and the bit left behind is the letter on the end.

blocks.note: Everyman is the setter's name, and it starts with E
very off-colour is VILE, of which most is the first three letters

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman signs nearly every puzzle he sets, so his name in a clue is almost always letters rather than a person — here just the one at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: wrong → EVIL: the far end of the same scale, where an act stops being a mistake and becomes wickedness.

clue.text: American lacking spirit - and never stout?

definitions.text: American lacking spirit - and never stout?

blocks.note: on the surface this is somebody with no fire or courage in them, which is the reading to let go of
not a remark about anybody's build: stout is a drink, and so is the spirit beside it
the nationality is really a spelling instruction, since the States write this word with one L where Britain uses two

explanation.walkthrough: Two drinks and no letters: spirit and stout both belong in a glass, and the person described is the one who touches neither of them.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue is the definition: somebody who takes no alcohol at all, spirits or beer, with the nationality fixing the single-L spelling.

clue.text: Scuttle, a bathroom fixture?

blocks.note: to scuttle a ship is to hole her deliberately and send her to the bottom
the plumbed basin, which takes its name from what the water does in it

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are about water going down, which is what hides the split: one is something you do to a ship, the other something bolted to a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Scuttle → SINK, the verb for putting a ship under on purpose; a bathroom fixture → SINK, the basin, so the clue uses a verb and a noun.

clue.text: Dance event, while getting maybe some bucks invested, finding singers

indicators.note: To invest is to clothe or wrap around, so what is invested ends up inside the letters rather than after them.

blocks.note: the dance event is a ball
while means as, the two swapping freely in 'while I was out'
bucks are male deer, and 'maybe' allows the general animal to stand for the particular one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bucks' is the pivot: dollars on the surface, animals in the wordplay, and 'maybe' is the flag saying one kind of deer stands for all.
explanation.definitionFit: singers → BALLADEERS: singers of ballads, the slow narrative songs, so the general word fairly covers the specialists.
